input:
Start-up
Before you bring the exchanger into service, walk the unit and satisfy yourself that the plate pack is correctly assembled, that the frame is closed up evenly, and that every connection to the exchanger is made and tight. Check that the gaskets are seated along the plates and that no gasket material is displaced or trapped where it does not belong. Set the vents and drains as the lineup requires, with the vents open for filling and the drains closed. Fill the cold side first, slowly, and let the air leave through the vent until a steady stream of liquid appears; then close the vent. Fill the hot side in the same patient way. Rushing the fill traps air in the pack, and trapped air shows itself later as poor heat transfer and misleading temperatures. With both sides full, look carefully along the plate pack edges and around every connection for leakage, and deal with any leak you find before heat is applied. Start the cold-side flow and establish it steadily, then bring in the hot-side flow gradually. Sudden flow changes slam the pack and stress the gaskets, so make every change in small steps and watch the temperatures and pressures respond between steps. As the outlet temperatures move toward their normal values, confirm that the flows are steady, that no new leakage has appeared, and that the instruments read consistently with one another. Only when the exchanger is full, vented, tight, and steady should you regard the start-up as complete and hand the unit over to normal operation. Take the transport covers and blanks off before you fill, and make sure nothing has been left inside a connection. Prove each vent and drain clear as you fill by the discharge you see from it. Fill each side on its own where the fluids differ, and let the pressure build with the flow rather than ahead of it, pausing as you go so that any leak has time to declare itself; a joint that looks dry early on can still weep once the unit is warm and flowing properly.
Normal operation
During normal operation, your task is to keep the exchanger inside its normal pattern of temperatures, flows, and pressure drops, and to notice departures from that pattern early. Read the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the flow on each side, and the pressure drop across the unit, and compare each reading with the pattern the exchanger has shown when clean and correctly lined up. Heat transfer that falls away while the pressure drop climbs is the familiar signature of fouling building on the plates. A pressure drop that rises suddenly points instead to a blockage or a wrongly set valve rather than to gradual fouling. Make changes to flow or temperature gradually, in small steps, because the plate pack and its gaskets answer sudden changes with stress they were not meant to carry. Keep the vents and drains closed and guarded while the unit is pressurised, and never loosen any part of the frame or any connection while pressure is on the exchanger. If leakage appears at the plate pack edge or at a connection, reduce the load on the unit and report the leak; do not attempt to correct leakage on a pressurised exchanger by tightening. Keep the area around the unit clear so that leaks are visible and access for inspection is not blocked. Record the readings at the routine rounds, because the trend across rounds, rather than any single reading, is what reveals fouling and drift. Read the readings as a set, because a change on one side shows up as a temperature change on the other. Judge the pressure drop at a steady flow, not while the flow is moving, and compare like with like between rounds, at the same flows where the duty allows. A gentle drift in the outlet temperatures at unchanged flows is heat transfer quietly going away, and that trend, not a single bad reading, is what justifies planning a cleaning opening.
Alarms
Two alarms are provided on this unit, and no others. The first is the high temperature alarm. When the high temperature alarm sounds, reduce the hot-side flow to cut the heat input, and check the cold-side flow and the position of the temperature control valve. If the temperature continues to rise after those actions, shut the hot side down and follow the shutdown procedure; do not hold a rising temperature by repeated small adjustments. The second is the low flow alarm. When the low flow alarm sounds, check that the pump on the affected side is running and that the valves in that line are open as the lineup requires. While the flow stays low, reduce the heat input to match the reduced flow. If the flow cannot be restored, shut the unit down in the normal order and report the cause before any restart. In both cases, acknowledge the alarm only after you have taken the stated action, and record the alarm, the action, and the result in the log. Whatever the alarm, act first and investigate in the order given; an alarm acknowledged and then left alone is worse than one left sounding, because the log then claims a response that never happened. If an alarm comes back after it has cleared, treat it as a new event and act again, and pass repeated alarms on in the record so that the next operator can see the pattern. Alarms are not to be silenced, bridged, or taken out of service to keep the unit running.
Shutdown
When you shut the exchanger down, reverse the order in which you started it. Reduce the hot-side flow first and let the heat input fall away, keeping the cold side flowing while the unit cools, because a hot, stagnant exchanger fouls and stresses its gaskets. When the temperatures have fallen toward the cold-side temperature, stop the hot-side flow completely, then stop the cold-side flow. Close the isolation valves on both sides. Open the vents and let the pressure fall to nothing before you open any drain, and confirm that the pressure has gone before you touch any connection. Drain both sides fully, and leave the unit drained and vented if it is to stand idle. Apply the locks and tags that the site practice requires for any later work on the unit. Report any leakage, damaged gasket, or distorted plate you noticed during the shutdown, and record the state in which the unit was left, so that the next start-up begins from a known condition. Once the unit is drained, look into the open connections for deposits, pieces of damaged gasket, and standing product, and put what you find in the shutdown record. If the pack is opened, support it as the frame comes off and keep the plates in their order. Store gaskets flat and out of heat and sunlight, and cover the open connections against dirt and weather, so that the unit you leave is one the next start-up can trust.
target:
Start-up
Inspect the exchanger before filling. Confirm that the plate pack is assembled correctly, the frame is closed evenly, the gaskets are seated, and every connection is made and tight. Set the vents open for filling and the drains closed. Fill the cold side slowly and vent the air until liquid flows steadily from the vent, then close the vent. Fill the hot side in the same way. A fast fill traps air in the pack; trapped air lowers heat transfer and falsifies the temperature readings. Check the plate pack edges and every connection for leakage with both sides full, and clear any leak before heat is applied. Establish the cold-side flow first and hold it steady. Bring the hot-side flow in gradually, in small steps, and watch the temperatures and pressures between steps; sudden changes stress the pack and the gaskets. The start-up is complete when the exchanger is full, vented, tight, and steady at its normal lineup, with the instruments in agreement. Remove the covers and blanks fitted for transport or storage before filling, and confirm that no tool, rag, or loose material has been left in any connection. Check that the drain and vent connections are clear by opening each briefly during filling and watching for a free discharge. Where the two sides carry different fluids, fill and vent each side separately and keep the sides separate throughout; a partly filled side reads as a false temperature pattern on the other side. Bring the pressure up with the flow, not ahead of it, and hold at each stage long enough for a leak to show. A joint that is dry at low flow may still weep when the flow and temperature reach their working pattern, and the start-up is not finished until the unit has been seen dry at that pattern.
Normal operation
Hold the exchanger at its normal pattern of temperatures, flows, and pressure drops, and read departures from that pattern early. Read the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the flow on each side, and the pressure drop across the unit at the routine rounds, and record the readings. The trend across rounds carries the information; a single reading does not. Falling heat transfer with a rising pressure drop is fouling on the plates. A sudden rise in pressure drop is a blockage or a wrongly set valve, not gradual fouling, and it is investigated as such. Make every change of flow or temperature gradually. Keep the vents and drains closed while the unit is pressurised. Never loosen the frame or any connection under pressure. A leak at the plate pack edge or at a connection is reported and the load on the unit is reduced; leakage is not corrected by tightening a pressurised exchanger. Keep access around the unit clear, so leaks stay visible and inspection is not blocked. Keep the two sides in balance as the process requires; a change made on one side appears as a temperature change on the other, and the readings are always read as a set. Watch the pressure drop at steady flow rather than during changes, because a changing flow moves the pressure drop for reasons that have nothing to do with the state of the plates. Where the duty allows, note the outlet temperatures at the same flows each round, so that rounds can be compared directly. A slow drift in outlet temperature at unchanged flows is heat transfer being lost, and it is planned for cleaning on the evidence of the trend, not on the evidence of a single poor reading. Do not wait for the duty to fail before acting on a clear trend, and do not open the unit on a weak one.
Alarms
Two alarms are provided, and no others. High temperature: reduce the hot-side flow to cut the heat input, and check the cold-side flow and the position of the temperature control valve. If the temperature continues to rise, shut the hot side down and follow the shutdown section; a rising temperature is not held by repeated small adjustments. Low flow: check that the pump on the affected side is running and that the valves in that line are open as the lineup requires. Reduce the heat input to match the reduced flow while the flow stays low. If the flow cannot be restored, shut the unit down in the normal order and report the cause before any restart. Acknowledge each alarm after the stated action has been taken, and record the alarm, the action, and the result in the log. Treat every alarm as an instruction to act first and to investigate in the order stated. An alarm that is acknowledged and left is worse than an alarm left sounding, because the record then shows a response that did not happen. If an alarm returns after the stated action has been taken and the condition has cleared, treat the return as a new event and repeat the stated action rather than assuming the first event is still running. Report repeated alarms at the end of the round, with the times taken from the log, so that a pattern of returns is visible to the next operator. No alarm is to be suppressed, bridged, or left out of service to keep the unit running.
Shutdown
Reduce the hot-side flow first and let the heat input fall away. Keep the cold side flowing while the unit cools; a hot, stagnant exchanger fouls and stresses its gaskets. When the temperatures have fallen toward the cold-side temperature, stop the hot-side flow, then stop the cold-side flow. Close the isolation valves on both sides. Open the vents and confirm that the pressure has fallen to nothing before any drain is opened or any connection is touched. Drain both sides fully. Leave the unit drained and vented if it is to stand idle, and apply the locks and tags the site practice requires for later work. Report any leakage, damaged gasket, or distorted plate found during the shutdown, and record the state in which the unit was left. The next start-up begins from the recorded state. After draining, look into the open connections for deposits, damaged gasket material, and product left standing in the pack, and report what is found with the shutdown record. If the unit is to be opened, support the plate pack as the frame is released and keep the plates in their order, because the order is part of the assembly. Keep gaskets flat and away from heat and sunlight while the unit stands open. Cover open connections against dirt and weather. A unit left drained, vented, clean inside its connections, and recorded as such can stand without attention; a unit left wet, sealed, and unrecorded cannot be trusted at the next start-up and is inspected as an unknown unit.
